turns.prompt:
You are given two attached CSV files describing perovskite solar cells as
complete devices — `substrate` (glass + transparent electrode), `etl`
(electron-transport layer stack), `htl` (hole-transport layer stack),
`backcontact` (metal / carbon back electrode), `deposition` (absorber
deposition procedure; `>>` separates steps). Every candidate below uses the
same MAPbI3 absorber in the same n-i-p (regular) architecture; they differ
only in the remaining columns. Each row is a device CONFIGURATION whose
efficiency is the median over at least 3 independently fabricated cells, so
it is a reproducible recipe rather than a single champion cell:
  - b3_pvk_stack_train.csv: 300 configurations with the measured power
    conversion efficiency (%).
  - b3_pvk_stack_pool.csv: 100 CANDIDATE configurations whose power
    conversion efficiency (%) was NOT measured, columns `candidate_id` and
    the same device columns.

Using the training data, select the 5 candidates with the HIGHEST power
conversion efficiency (%).

Reason from the device physics — band alignment and selectivity of the
transport layers, interface recombination, contact chemistry and the film
quality the process is likely to give — then end your answer with an
explicit ranked list of candidate_ids, best first, e.g. "Final: c901, c902,
c903, c904, c905".
turns.answer_text:
My predicted top five are **c064, c083, c043, c013, and c017**. I prioritize complementary electron/hole selectivity and interface passivation, using the measured configurations as anchors rather than assuming that any particular material guarantees high efficiency.

| Rank | Candidate | Training evidence and device-physics rationale |
|---|---|---|
| **1** | **c064** | **Strongest high-efficiency ETL analogue.** The same `TiO2-c | SnO2-np` / Spiro-MeOTAD combination reaches **20.85%** in training, although with Ag and an additional dip-coating step. Another `TiO2-c | SnO2` device reaches **17.47%** with spin-coating alone. Compact TiO₂ can block holes and electrode shunts, while the absorber-facing SnO₂ provides favorable electron extraction. Spiro-MeOTAD/Au supplies a complementary hole-selective contact. I would not transfer the full 20.85% result without the process step, but this remains a particularly strong candidate. |
| **2** | **c083** | **Promising electron-interface passivation.** Dimethylbiguanide has nitrogen-containing groups that could coordinate under-coordinated lead and modify the TiO₂/perovskite interface dipole. A sufficiently thin layer could reduce trap-assisted recombination without obstructing extraction. The training data support the broader strategy: `TiO2-c | Graphene-QDs` reaches **17.405%**, and several modified oxide/fullerene interfaces reach approximately **17–18%**. This is the most extrapolative selection: coverage, protonation, and thickness would determine whether the modification helps. |
| **3** | **c043** | **Passivated hole contact on an established mesoporous stack.** It retains compact/mesoporous TiO₂, Spiro-MeOTAD, and Au, with DAHI at the absorber/HTL interface. If that modifier suppresses surface recombination while preserving hole transfer, both voltage and fill factor can benefit. Closely related training configurations with `PMMA | Spiro-MeOTAD` and `PbS-QDs | Spiro-MeOTAD` achieve **18.01%** and **18.63%**, respectively. |
| **4** | **c013** | **Interfacial polarization plus a favorable metal-contact buffer.** A thin P(VDF-TrFE) layer could screen interfacial charge and reduce recombination; excessive thickness would instead impede hole extraction. Spiro-MeOTAD provides hole transport, and MoO₃ can improve coupling to Ag. The analogous *interfacial modifier / Spiro-MeOTAD / MoO₃–Ag* configuration using IEICO-4F reaches **18.965%** in training, supporting this contact strategy, though not an identical polymer effect. |
| **5** | **c017** | **The closest complete-stack high-performance match.** After normalizing capitalization, the training set contains essentially the same fullerene electron-contact stack, doped TaTm hole-contact stack, and co-evaporation process at **17.9%**, with Au rather than Ag. Selective fullerene extraction, a conductive doped HTL, and controlled evaporated-film formation make this a comparatively well-supported choice. Ag introduces contact-chemistry uncertainty but does not eliminate that strong analogue. |

These are predictions, not measured pool efficiencies. In particular, the generic deposition labels omit annealing, solvent, thickness, and interlayer-coverage details, so the exact ordering is less certain than the underlying shortlist.

Final: c064, c083, c043, c013, c017
